key: There is no suffering for him who has finished his journey, and abandoned grief, who has freed himself on all sides, and thrown off all fetters.
s: Opening a chapter on the venerable, the verse names who is past pain; the Theravāda commentary, on verse 90, takes the suffering that ceases as the mind’s fever, for heat and cold still reach the body even of one whose cankers are destroyed.

evidence.words: Pariḷāho na vijjatīti duvidho pariḷāho kāyiko cetasiko cāti. Tesu khīṇāsavassa sītuṇhādivasena uppannattā kāyikapariḷāho anibbutova, taṃ sandhāya jīvako pucchati. Satthā pana dhammarājatāya desanāvidhikusalatāya cetasikapariḷāhavasena desanaṃ vinivattento, ‘‘jīvaka, paramatthena evarūpassa khīṇāsavassa pariḷāho na vijjatī’’ti āha.
evidence.gloss: ‘No fever (suffering) exists’: fever is of two kinds, bodily and mental. Of these, in one whose cankers are destroyed the bodily fever, arising by way of cold, heat and the like, is not quenched, and it was of this that Jīvaka asked. But the Teacher, as king of the Dhamma and skilled in the ways of teaching, turned the teaching to mental fever and said, ‘Jīvaka, in the highest sense no fever exists for one whose cankers are destroyed, such as this.’
